text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, whose governments are at odds over the Palestinian peace process, met on Tuesday and described the talks as businesslike and useful.
"That was a serious and very frank talk about the (peace) process...the obstacles," Moussa told journalists after the talks on the fringes of an European security summit in Lisbon.
"We listened to what...Mr Netanyahu had to say. It was a very useful and businesslike meeting," he said about the discussions, that lasted for over an hour.
"They went very well," echoed Netanyahu. "We discussed all aspects of the peace process in the Middle East," he said.

Israel and the Palestinian authorities, supported by their Arab backers, have traded accusations over who is to blame for stalling the peace process, which ran into problems after Netanyahu's right-wing government took office in Tel Aviv in June.

The Arabs charge Israel with dragging its feet over the scheduled withdrawal of troops from the West Bank city of Hebron and say that it is reneging on commitments to trade occupied Arab land for peace.
But Netanyahu says that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat has been delaying a final deal on Hebron in the hope of extracting more concessions.
"Of course we have a number of differences and points of view, but I think there was a real desire to understand one another," Netanyahu said.
Moussa said that he had delivered a letter to Netanyahu from Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and had received a written reply in return.
"We hope we can overcome the obstacles in a fair way... to reach a balanced agreement that would satisfy both sides," Moussa said.
